Each problem set in this course will ask you to address three types of questions:

* **The gimmes**: The first few questions of each problem set ask you to do things like name your R file and load the tidyverse.

* **Straight from the course material**: Most questions will directly reflect the material as it was provided.

* **Integrated questions**: Some questions ask you to integrate material from across the course and/or test your conceptual understanding. Avoid getting stuck asking yourself, "*Where did we do this?*" That question can become a time sink when you are being asked to apply functions in a new way. Taking careful notes during the lectures can help. Additionally, review the functions guide at the end of each module!

## Recommended workflow

**Do not begin by coding your way through the problems!** Data wrangling is the process of solving a series of puzzles, and jumping straight to the code can become a *major* time sink. Instead, *plan ahead* — a whiteboard, pencil, and scrap paper are among a coder's most important problem-solving tools.

Here is my recommended workflow for solving problem sets:

::: {.workflow-list}
1. **Functions that you may use**: Start by reviewing the "Functions that you may use …" list. If any functions are unfamiliar, place the cursor within the function name and press [F1]{.mono}, or run a help command such as `?mean`. Then use RStudio's Find in Files command ([Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + F]{.mono}) to search your code-along scripts and course tutorials for examples of how we have used the function.

2. **Explore the data**: Before heading to the questions (other than data loading), explore the dataset using functions such as `str()` and `summary()`. Pay careful attention to the class and type of values present, the container used to hold those values (e.g., a list or atomic vector), and whether there are any [NA]{.mono} values. Unless you are explicitly asked to do so, do not include data-exploration code in your submitted assignment.

3. **Visualize**: For each question, visualize what you want the resulting object to look like. Look for clues in the language of the question to determine the *class* of the resulting object (e.g., should it be a single value or a data frame?).

4. **Write out the primary steps** (*integrated questions*): If you are confronted with an *integrated question*, use pencil and paper or a whiteboard to plan the primary steps needed to achieve the result. I am a visual thinker, so I typically create diagrams that resemble flowcharts. You can also write out the steps using plain language that a non-coder could understand.

5. **Add the individual stages** (*integrated questions*): Expand your plan using pencil and paper or a whiteboard by breaking each multi-step process into individual stages. Continue using a diagram or plain language. Be specific at this stage (e.g., "subset the rows of the data frame using a logical test").

6. **Add candidate functions** (*integrated questions*): Once you are confident that your plan is complete, add candidate functions from the *approved* functions list to each stage. Give this step careful consideration. For example, to subset a data frame, use the `select()` family to choose columns, the `slice()` family to choose rows by position, or the `filter()` family to choose rows using a logical condition. Look for clues in the question that point to an appropriate family of functions. Adding or modifying a variable suggests `mutate()`, whereas calculating a summary value for a dataset or group suggests `summarize()`.

7. **Code it**: Then (and only then) should you address a problem with code! *Note: When you do so, avoid removing the question text or section headers.*

8. **Test it**: Make sure the output matches what you expected:

    * If a multi-step process does not generate the expected output (or throws an error), highlight and run individual sections of the code to verify that each component produces the desired result.
    * If the process includes iteration or a custom function, temporarily assign a representative value to the index or argument name in the global environment (e.g., `i`, `x`, or `.x`) and test the expression outside the loop or function. *Avoid making wholesale changes to the entire code block without first testing its individual components.*
:::

While the first step is specific to our problem sets, steps 2–8 are also useful when solving data-wrangling problems outside this course.

## Other tips and tricks {.compact-section-end}

You can protect your problem set score by following these practices:

* Always ensure that the naming convention used for your assignment is [problem_set\_\[week\]\_\[last\_name\]\_\[first\_name\].R]{.mono}. For example, if I submitted a problem set for the first week, the name of my submitted document would be [problem_set_1_evans_brian.R]{.mono}.

* Never, never, never use `setwd()`!

* Always use keyboard shortcuts for adding global assignment operators ([Alt/Option + Dash]{.mono}), comments ([Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + C]{.mono}), and pipes ([Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M]{.mono}).

* Before submitting your problem set:

    * Select all content ([Ctrl/Cmd + A]{.mono}) and fix any potential indentation errors with the keyboard shortcut [Ctrl/Cmd + I]{.mono}.

    * Double-check your code formatting using the [***Course style guide***](https://evansbrians.github.io/gis_2026/resources/course_style_guide/){target="_blank"}.

    * Cross-check your functions (including operators) with those provided to you in the "Functions you may use …" section.

    * Clear your global environment or restart R (Menu bar → Session → Restart R) and run your entire script. If it runs without errors, you are ready to submit it through Canvas!

## Submitting your problem set {.mt-0}

Submit your completed R script file (`.R`) through the appropriate weekly assignment in Canvas. Do not submit the HTML problem set or its associated data files unless the assignment explicitly instructs you to do so.

1. In Canvas, open the course and select **Assignments** in the Course Navigation menu.
2. Open the correct problem-set assignment, verify its title and due date, and select **Start Assignment**.
3. Select the **File Upload** tab and choose your completed `.R` script. Confirm that the displayed filename follows the required naming convention.
4. Select **Submit Assignment**.
5. Verify that Canvas displays the submission details. Use the link to the submitted file to download or open it and confirm that you uploaded the correct script.

Canvas provides illustrated instructions for [submitting an online assignment](https://community.instructure.com/en/kb/articles/661210-how-do-i-submit-an-online-assignment){target="_blank"} and [uploading a file as an assignment submission](https://community.instructure.com/en/kb/articles/661219-how-do-i-upload-a-file-as-an-assignment-submission-in-canvas){target="_blank"}. The Canvas interface may look slightly different if Assignment Enhancements are enabled, but the general submission process is the same.

## Using external coding resources

### A note on Stack Overflow

Stack Overflow can be a valuable resource, but **I strongly advise against using it when completing weekly problem sets**. Anyone can answer a question, older answers may rely on superseded R workflows, and searching can become a major time sink. For problem sets, begin with the course materials, the approved functions list, and the Canvas discussion board.

### A note on AI

You are welcome to use AI tools, such as ChatGPT or Claude, to help you complete problem sets. We strongly recommend using AI as a thought partner rather than as a source of answers. AI-generated R code may rely on outdated workflows, deprecated functions, or functions that are not included in the approved functions list. Carefully review and test any AI-generated suggestions — you are responsible for writing, reviewing, understanding, and verifying every line of code that you submit.
